title: Burns & Environmental

learn.summary: Heat, cold, and sun injuries share a theme: the first-aid response is simple, but recognizing severity is what saves lives. Cooling a burn correctly, telling heat exhaustion from heat stroke, and spotting hypothermia early are all pattern-recognition skills you can genuinely build before ever taking a course — then call 911 when the severe pattern appears.

do: Learn the one-liner 'cool the burn with running water for 20 minutes' and post it inside a kitchen cabinet door this week.

children.title: Burn Degrees & Cooling

learn.summary: First-degree burns are red and painful (sunburn-like); second-degree blister; third-degree look white, leathery, or charred and may not hurt because nerves are destroyed. Treatment for minor burns: cool running water — not ice, not butter, not toothpaste — for 20 minutes, then loose sterile covering. Call 911 or seek emergency care for third-degree burns, burns bigger than the person's palm, or any burn to face, hands, genitals, or airway.

do: Quiz yourself tonight: name the three degrees, the cooling time, and three things never to put on a burn — out loud, from memory.

children.title: Heat Exhaustion vs Stroke

learn.summary: Heat exhaustion: heavy sweating, pale clammy skin, nausea, dizziness — move to shade, sip water, cool with wet cloths; recovery in 30 minutes is expected. Heat stroke is a 911 emergency: body temperature at or above 103°F (39.4°C), hot skin that may be dry, confusion, or loss of consciousness — cool aggressively (ice packs to neck, armpits, groin; immersion if possible) while waiting, and give nothing to drink to a confused person.

do: Memorize the deciding line — 'confusion means call 911' — and share it with whoever you exercise or work outdoors with.

children.title: Hypothermia & Frostbite

learn.summary: Hypothermia (core below 95°F/35°C) announces itself with the 'umbles' — stumbles, mumbles, fumbles, grumbles — and paradoxically, shivering stopping is a sign of worsening, not improvement. Handle victims gently, get them dry and insulated, and warm the core before the limbs. Frostbite: never rub the tissue and never rewarm if refreezing is possible; use body heat or water at 98.6–102°F (37–39°C), not direct flame or heaters.

do: Add a packable insulation layer and a beanie to your car or day-hike bag this week — most hypothermia cases happen in air temperatures above freezing.

children.title: Sun Protection

learn.summary: Sunburn is a first-degree radiation burn, and five or more blistering sunburns in youth roughly doubles melanoma risk. The evidence-backed basics: broad-spectrum SPF 30+, applied 15 minutes before exposure and reapplied every 2 hours (or after swimming), plus shade in the 10 a.m.–4 p.m. window and a real hat. Most people apply about half the tested amount — a full shot-glass worth covers an adult body.

do: Check your sunscreen's expiry date today (typically 3 years) and put a bottle somewhere you'll actually use it — car, bag, or desk.
